title: HTML Lists and Tables
subtitle: Organize information like professional dashboards
description: Learn ordered lists, unordered lists, nested lists, description lists, and build professional tables with thead, tbody, tfoot, captions and accessibility - exactly what your final app dashboard will need.

blocks.text: Why lists and tables power every app you use

Look at any app: YouTube has list of videos, Jumia has list of products, your bank app has table of transactions, Code Academy has list of lessons and table of progress. Lists and tables are how we organize information so humans can scan quickly. Today your portfolio becomes organized and scannable.
Open Menu > Practical now. You will create 3 things today: a skills list, a projects timeline, and a pricing table. These will go directly into your final complete app.
Unordered lists - when order doesn't matter

Use ul when order doesn't matter - like skills, features, ingredients. Each item is li. Browser adds bullet points by default. But semantic meaning is: this is a collection of related items where sequence is not important. That's why we use ul for navigation menus in Lesson 3 - nav items are related but order is not strictly sequential.

blocks.text: Ordered lists - when sequence matters

Use ol when order DOES matter - steps, rankings, timeline. Browser adds numbers 1,2,3. You can control numbering with type attribute: type="A" for A,B,C, type="a" for a,b,c, type="I" for Roman I,II,III, type="i" for i,ii,iii. Also start attribute to start from different number, and reversed to count backwards.

blocks.text: Nested lists - lists inside lists for real menus

Real apps have nested navigation - like Courses > HTML > Lesson 1, Lesson 2. You achieve this by putting ul or ol INSIDE li. Important: The nested list must be inside the li, not directly inside ul. This is where many beginners make invalid HTML.

blocks.text: Description lists - the hidden gem for portfolios

Most tutorials skip dl, dt, dd but professionals use it daily. dl = description list, dt = term, dd = description of term. Perfect for FAQs, glossary, project details like Client: Code Academy, Year: 2026. Much more semantic than using p or div for term-description pairs.

blocks.text: Tables - not for layout, for data

Old websites used tables for layout - that's WRONG today. Tables are ONLY for tabular data like price lists, schedules, transaction history. A table has table wrapper, caption for title, thead for header row, tbody for data rows, tfoot for footer/summary, tr for row, th for header cell, td for data cell.
Critical: th must have scope attribute - scope="col" for column header, scope="row" for row header. This helps screen readers announce table correctly. Without scope, blind users get lost in tables.

blocks.text: Colspan and Rowspan - merging cells like Excel

Sometimes cell needs to span multiple columns or rows. colspan="2" means this cell takes 2 columns width, rowspan="2" means 2 rows height. Use for summary rows, merged headers, complex data. But don't overuse - complex spanning hurts accessibility.

blocks.question: You need to show steps to deploy website: 1) Buy domain 2) Write HTML 3) Upload. Which list type and why?
options: <ul> because steps are collection of items and ul is default for any collection, order doesn't matter for deployment steps
<ol> because sequence matters - you must buy domain before uploading, order is critical to meaning, ol conveys sequential order semantically
<dl> because steps are terms and descriptions, so dl with dt for step number and dd for action is correct
<table> because steps should be in table with Step Number column and Action column for better structure
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct! ul = unordered collection, ol = ordered sequence. Deployment steps are sequential - order changes meaning.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Ask: If you swap step 1 and 3, does meaning change? If yes, order matters.
blocks.reasoning: ol is for sequential order where sequence matters. ul is for collection where order doesn't matter. Deployment steps are ordered.

blocks.question: You build pricing table with <td> for all cells including header row 'Feature, Starter, Business'. Screen reader user says it's confusing. What semantic fix makes table accessible?
options: Change header cells to <th scope="col"> and row headers to <th scope="row"> and add <caption> and use <thead> <tbody> because th with scope tells screen readers header relationship and caption gives table title
Add <b> to header cells to make them bold because screen readers announce bold as header
Add id attribute to each td because screen readers need id to identify headers
Wrap table in <nav> because tables are navigation and nav provides landmark
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent accessibility! th + scope + caption + thead/tbody is what WCAG requires for data tables.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: How do screen readers know which cell is header for which data? What attribute defines header scope?
blocks.reasoning: th denotes header cell, scope=col/row defines relationship, caption provides title, thead/tbody provide structure for assistive tech.

blocks.question: You need FAQ section: Question 'What is HTML?' Answer 'Structure language'. Which markup is most semantic and why not use ul or p?
options:
• What is HTML?
  • Structure language
because ul is for any question-answer pair

What is HTML?

Structure language

because p with bold is simplest and most compatible
<dl><dt>What is HTML?</dt><dd>Structure language</dd></dl> because dl is specifically designed for term-description and question-answer pairs, conveying association semantically

What is HTML?Structure language
because FAQ should be in table for alignment
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! dl is the hidden gem for FAQ, glossary, key-value pairs. ul and p lose the semantic association.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Which element is designed for term and its description? Not ul (collection) nor table (tabular data).
blocks.reasoning: dl = description list, dt = term/question, dd = description/answer. It semantically links them, unlike ul or separate p tags.

blocks.question: You have table with Total: 160 XP in a 3-column table. It renders but layout looks off in some browsers. What is critical rule for colspan and accessibility?
options: colspan is deprecated in HTML5 and should be replaced with CSS grid, that's why layout breaks
colspan value must not exceed remaining columns in row and you must ensure total columns per row still matches table structure, and use th with scope for total label for accessibility
colspan only works in thead not tbody, so move total row to thead to fix layout
colspan requires rowspan to be present as well, you must add rowspan="1" whenever you use colspan
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect table mastery! Colspan math and accessibility matters for production tables.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: If table has 3 columns and you colspan 2, how many columns does that row have? Does it match others?
blocks.reasoning: colspan merges columns, but row's total column count must remain consistent. Also header for total should be th scope=row for accessibility.

blocks.text: Your app is now organized like a dashboard

You now know ul for unordered collections, ol for ordered sequences with type/start/reversed, nested lists must be inside li, dl for term-description and FAQ, tables with caption, thead, tbody, tfoot, th scope, colspan/rowspan. Your portfolio now has skills list, timeline, pricing table, and project details - exactly what clients want to see.
